title: Wyandot on Kentucky’s northern frontier
summary: The Wyandot hunted and camped in Kentucky from towns north of the Ohio, and in August 1782 their warriors fought at Bryan Station and Blue Licks.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Wyandot](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wyandot_people) came out of the Wendat, or Huron, peoples of the Great Lakes. They spoke an Iroquoian language. In the 1640s the Haudenosaunee broke up the Wendat confederacy in the [Beaver Wars](/stories/iroquois-beaver-wars/), and survivors moved west and regrouped. By the 1700s their towns stood near Detroit and along the Sandusky in what is now Ohio.

From there they still used the Kentucky country. Hunting parties crossed the Ohio in the cold months to take deer, bear, and buffalo and to make salt. Historian A. Gwynn Henderson's [study of Indian life in Kentucky](https://preservationkentucky.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Dispelling-the-Myth-17th-18th-Century-Indian-Life-in-KY.pdf) counts the Wyandot among the nations who hunted and camped here. No Wyandot camp site in Kentucky is documented in the sources cited here.

When the Revolution came, many Wyandot sided with Britain, whose officers at Detroit supplied the war parties. Kentucky's stations were new and close. The Wyandot fought to keep their hunting ground.

Their best-known fight here came in August 1782. Wyandot warriors joined Shawnee and Lenape fighters and [Capt. William Caldwell's](/people/#william-caldwell) Rangers in the [siege of Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) near Lexington. [Simon Girty](/stories/simon-girty-interpreter-at-bryan-station-1782/) rode with them. The siege failed, and the war party pulled back north.

Kentucky militia chased them. Three days later, at the Lower Blue Licks, the warriors were waiting. The [Battle of Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/) lasted only minutes. Col. [John Todd](/people/#john-todd), Col. [Stephen Trigg](/people/#stephen-trigg), and [Israel Boone](/people/#israel-boone), Daniel Boone's son, were among the dead. It was one of the worst defeats Kentucky settlers ever took.

The Wyandot kept fighting into the 1790s and signed the [Treaty of Greenville](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/) in 1795. Later treaties pushed them out of Ohio. In 1843 they moved west to Kansas, and many later moved on to Oklahoma.

Treat them as their own nation in the record, not a footnote to a generic "Indian raid." Their own name for this land is told in the [story of Kah-ten-tah-teh](/stories/wyandot-name-kah-ten-tah-teh-fair-land-of-tomorrow/).

## Kentucky today

Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park in Robertson County marks the 1782 fight. The [Wyandotte Nation](https://wyandotte-nation.org/culture/our-history/) of Oklahoma carries the Wyandot story forward today.
